## Overview

This analysis evaluates transcriptional variations on {{< acr chrX >}} between male and female individuals to uncover sex-specific dynamics. This study utilizes a cohort of 12 paired-end {{< acr RNAseq >}} samples obtained from distinct geographical populations. By adjusting for population structure, this analysis isolates robust sex-linked genetic expression underlying chromosome-wide regulation mechanisms.

## Methods

### Data Processing

Raw paired-end sequencing reads were processed using a reproducible, custom Nextflow DSL2 pipeline hosted at [github.com/DevonAllies/rnaseq-pipeline](https://github.com/DevonAllies/rnaseq_pipeline/tree/main). The computational workflow was systemically executed using the following steps:

| Step | Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| {{< acr QC >}} | FastQC | Assess raw read quality |
| Adapter trimming | Trim Galore | Remove sequencing adapters |
| Alignment | HISAT2 | Splice-aware alignment to {{< acr chrX >}} |
| Assembly | StringTie | Per-sample transcript quantification |
| Merging | StringTie merge | Consensus transcriptome across samples |
| Re-estimation | StringTie | Re-quantify against merged {{< acr GTF >}} |
| {{< acr QC >}} report | MultiQC | Aggregate quality metrics |

The pipeline execution was controlled via the baseline terminal command:

```bash
nextflow run rnaseq.nf -profile local --hisat2_prefix indexes/chrX_tran
```
### Differential Expression

Downstream {{< acr DE >}} modeling was performed at the gene level using the [Ballgown](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/ballgown.html) R package. To isolate sexual differences, phenotypic sex was treated as the primary covariate. Population origin was strictly embedded as a confounding adjustment variable to account for ancestry-driven batch effects. Statistical significance was controlled using {{< acr FDR >}} threshold of $q-value < 0.05$.

## Setup and Sample Phenotypes

### Sample Population Metrics

```{r}
#| label: libraries
#| results: hide

packages <- c("tidyverse", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "ballgown", "genefilter", "ggrepel")
lapply(packages, library, character.only = TRUE)
```

::: {.content-visble when-format="pdf"}
\newpage
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-phenodata
#| tbl-cap: "Sample phenotype information"

# load sample metadata
pheno_data <- read.csv("data/geuvadis_phenodata.csv")

# Match sample IDs to directory names
pheno_data$ids <- paste0(pheno_data$ids, "_chrX")

pheno_data |>
  knitr::kable(booktabs = TRUE) |> 
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_option = c("hold_position", "striped"),
    font_size = 9
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: sample-summary

yri_male <- pheno_data$ids[pheno_data$population == "YRI" & pheno_data$sex == "male"]
yri_female <- pheno_data$ids[pheno_data$population == "YRI" & pheno_data$sex == "female"]
gbr_male <- pheno_data$ids[pheno_data$population == "GBR" & pheno_data$sex == "male"]
gbr_female <- pheno_data$ids[pheno_data$population == "GBR" & pheno_data$sex == "female"]

n_total <- nrow(pheno_data)
```

The sample group balances phenotypic sex and regional cohorts across `r n_total` distinct repository entries. The baseline experimental structure is detailed below: 

- **YRI Cohort:** Comprises `r length(yri_male)` male samples (`r paste(yri_male, collapse = ", ")`) and `r length(yri_female)` female samples (`r paste(yri_female, collapse = ", ")`).

- **GBR Cohort:** Comprises `r length(gbr_male)` male samples (`r paste(gbr_male, collapse = ", ")`) and `r length(gbr_female)` female samples (`r paste(gbr_female, collapse = ", ")`).

```{r}
#| label: load-ballgown
#| results: hide

# Load Ballgown object from StringTie ctab files
bg <- ballgown(
  dataDir = "data/stringtie_final",
  samplePattern = "ERR",
  pData = pheno_data
)

# Filter low-abundance transcripts
bg_filtered <- subset(bg, "rowVars(texpr(bg)) > 1", genomesubset = TRUE)
```

## Exploratory Analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca
#| fig-cap: "PCA of transcript-level FPKM expression across all chrX samples"

# Extract FPKM matrix and remove zero-variance rows
fpkm_mat <- texpr(bg, "FPKM")
fpkm_log <- log(fpkm_mat + 1)
fpkm_var <- fpkm_log[rowVars(fpkm_log) > 0, ]

# PCA
pca <- prcomp(t(fpkm_var), scale. = TRUE)

pca_df <- as.data.frame(pca$x) |>
  mutate(
    sex        = pData(bg)$sex,
    population = pData(bg)$population,
    sample     = sampleNames(bg)
  )

# Variance explained
var_exp <- round(summary(pca)$importance[2, 1:2] * 100, 1)

ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2,
                   colour = sex, shape = population,
                   label = sample)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text_repel(size = 3, max.overlaps = 20) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("female" = "#E91E8C", "male" = "#1E90E9"),
    guide  = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 4, alpha = 1))
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("GBR" = 15, "YRI" = 17)) +
  labs(
    title  = "PCA of RNA-seq Expression (chrX)",
    x      = paste0("PC1 (", var_exp[1], "% variance)"),
    y      = paste0("PC2 (", var_exp[2], "% variance)"),
    colour = "Sex",
    shape  = "Population"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

```{r}
#| label: de-analysis
#| results: hide

# Transcript-level DE by sex, adjusting for population
results_transcripts <- stattest(
  bg_filtered,
  feature = "transcript",
  covariate = "sex",
  adjustvars = "population",
  getFC = TRUE,
  meas = "FPKM"
)

# Gene-level DE
results_genes <- stattest(
  bg_filtered,
  feature = "gene",
  covariate = "sex",
  adjustvars = "population",
  getFC = TRUE,
  meas = "FPKM"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: significant-genes

# Add gene names to results
results_transcripts <- data.frame(
  geneNames = geneNames(bg_filtered),
  geneIDs = geneIDs(bg_filtered),
  results_transcripts
)

# Filter significant genes at q < 0.05
sig_genes <- results_genes |> 
  filter(qval < 0.05) |> 
  arrange(qval)

# Filter significant transcript at q < 0.05
sig_transcripts <- results_transcripts |> 
  filter(qval < 0.05) |> 
  arrange(qval)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-volcano
#| fig-cap: "Volcano plots of differential gene expression on chrX. Fold change is calculated male relative to female, adjusted for population (YRI and GBR). Dashed horizontal line indicates q = 0.05 significance threshold."

results_genes |>
  mutate(
    log2fc    = log2(fc),
    neg_log10 = -log10(qval),
    sig       = qval < 0.05,
    label     = case_when(
      id == "MSTRG.332" ~ "XIST",
      id == "MSTRG.331" ~ "TSIX",
      id == "MSTRG.233" ~ "KDM6A",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log2fc, y = neg_log10, colour = sig)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1),     linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), size = 3.5, na.rm = TRUE, fontface = "italic") +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "grey60", "TRUE" = "#d73027"),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "No", "TRUE" = "Yes"),
    guide  = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 4, alpha = 1))
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = max(log2(results_genes$fc), na.rm = TRUE),
           y = -log10(0.05) + 0.1, label = "q = 0.05",
           hjust = 1, size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(
    x        = expression(log[2]~"Fold Change"),
    y        = expression(-log[10]~"(q-value)"),
    title    = "Differential Expression on Chromosome X",
    subtitle = "Male vs Female | Adjusted for population",
    colour   = "Significant"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxplots
#| fig-cap: "Expression of significant Chromosome X genes by sex (FPKM)"

# Extract FPKM expression matrix
fpkm <- texpr(bg_filtered, meas = "FPKM")

# Extract before piping
fpkm_t <- as.data.frame(t(fpkm))

fpkm_df <- fpkm_t |>
  mutate(
    sample = rownames(fpkm_t),
    sex    = pheno_data$sex
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = -c(sample, sex),
    names_to  = "transcript_id",
    values_to = "fpkm"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    transcript_num = as.integer(transcript_id),
    gene = case_when(
      transcript_num == 1059 ~ "XIST",
      transcript_num == 1058 ~ "TSIX",
      transcript_num == 435  ~ "KDM6A",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(gene))

ggplot(fpkm_df, aes(x = sex, y = log2(fpkm + 1), fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 1, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("female" = "#d73027", "male" = "#4575b4")) +
  labs(
    x     = "Sex",
    y     = expression(log[2]~"(FPKM + 1)"),
    title = "Expression of Significant Chromosome X Genes by Sex"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Results

### Transcript Filtering

An initial set of `r format(nrow(texpr(bg)), big.mark = ",")` transcripts was extracted from the StringTie quantification step. To eliminate uninformative background noise and improve statistical power, transcripts with low variance across samples were pruned. Applying a filtration cutoff threshold of $rowVar > 1$ successfully yielded `r format(nrow(texpr(bg_filtered)), big.mark = ",")` high-confidence transcripts retained for exploratory and differential expression processing.

### Exploratory Variance Analysis

To understand global relationship structures within the filtered datasets, a {{< acr PCA >}} was calculated on transcript-level {{< acr FPKM >}} expression data.

As plotted in @fig-pca, the first two principal components explained `r var_exp[1] + var_exp[2]`% of total variance (PC1: `r var_exp[1]`%, PC2: `r var_exp[2]`%). The distribution patterns reveal a modest separation based on biological sex along the axis trajectories. Concurrently, clear macro-clusters demonstrate underlying population structure, showing distinct spatial partitioning between European (GBR) and African (YRI) cohorts. This population grouping confirms the necessity of utilizing nested model adjustments within the F-test framework to avoid ancestry-driven false-positive discoveries.

### Differential Expression

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sig-transcripts
#| tbl-cap: "Significant differentially expressed transcripts (q < 0.05)"

sig_transcripts |> 
  mutate(
    fc   = round(fc, 3),
    pval = format(pval, scientific = TRUE, digits = 2),
    qval = format(qval, scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(booktabs = TRUE) |> 
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_option = c("hold_position", "striped"),
    font_size = 9
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sig-genes
#| tbl-cap: "Significant differentially expressed genes (q < 0.05)"

sig_genes |>  
  mutate(
    fc   = round(fc, 3),
    pval = format(pval, scientific = TRUE, digits = 2),
    qval = format(qval, scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(booktabs = TRUE) |> 
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_option = c("hold_position", "striped"),
    font_size = 9
  )
```

Statistical testing on the curated genomic features revealed a highly localized set of differentially expressed targets. As mapped out in @fig-volcano, only three specific genes crossed the designated horizontal significance threshold of $q = 0.05$. Fold-change computations reflect expression levels of males relative to females; consequently, negative log~2~ fold-change parameters pinpoint strong female-biased gene expression patterns.

The three significant genes identified are:

```{r}
#| label: sig_gen-values

xist <- sig_genes[sig_genes$id == "MSTRG.332", ]
tsix <- sig_genes[sig_genes$id == "MSTRG.331", ]
kdm6a <- sig_genes[sig_genes$id == "MSTRG.233", ]

# Format q-values as proper scientific notations for inline use
fmt_q <- function(q) {
  s <- format(q, scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)
  parts <- strsplit(s, "e")[[1]]
  paste0(parts[1], " \\times 10^{", as.integer(parts[2]), "}")
}
```

- **XIST (MSTRG.332):** Shows an extreme female bias with a fold change value of `r round(xist$fc, 5)` and a significance score ($q = `r fmt_q(xist$qval)`$).

- **TSIX (MSTRG.331):** Displays an aligned female bias with an intermediate fold change metric of `r round(tsix$fc, 5)` ($q = `r fmt_q(tsix$qval)`$).

- **KDM6A (MSTRG.233):** Reaches significant separation parameters with an adjusted fold change value of `r round(kdm6a$fc, 5)` ($q = `r fmt_q(kdm6a$qval)`$).

### Gene Abundance Quantification

To validate individual candidate patterns, expression profiles were plotted using log~2~ ({{< acr FPKM >}} + 1) metrics. The resulting boxplots (@fig-boxplots) illustrate clear group distributions:

- **XIST and TSIX Expression:** Both features exhibit definitive binary regulation profiles. Abundance levels are highly elevated in females (with median log~2~ values resting between 6.0 and 9.0) but drop down to zero baseline noise across all male samples. This is consistent with their known roles: _XIST_ drives female-specific {{< acr XCI >}}, while _TSIX_ acts as its antisense regulator partner.

- **KDM6A Expression:** Unlike the regulatory {{< acr RNA >}},  _KDM6A_ is actively transcribed in both sexes. However, female samples present a statistically elevated expression ceiling compared to male profiles. This matches its classification as an {{< acr XCI >}}-escape gene that regularly maintains dual-dosage activity in female tissue.

## Discussion and Conclusion

### Biological Implications of Female-Biased Expression

The differential expression analysis of human Chromosome X transcripts revealed a highly localized regulatory signature. Only three genes - _XIST_, _TSIX_, and _KDM6A_ - exhibited statistically  significant expression differences between sexes ($q < 0.05$). All three candidates demonstrated explicit female-biased abundance. This tight localization underscores the stringent evolutionary conservation governing sex-chromosome dosage mechanisms in humans.

### Mechanistic Synergy of XIST and TSIX

The identification of XIST (MSTRG.332) and TSIX (MSTRG.331) as the most statistically significant differentially expressed features aligns with established models of
{{< acr XCI >}} [@Lyon1961; @Galupa2018]. In female mammals, dosage compensation between XX and XY individuals is achieved by transcriptionally silencing one of the two female X chromosomes.

- **XIST Function:** This {{< acr lncRNA >}} is transcribed exclusively from the future inactive X chromosome ($X_i$). It physically coats the chromosome in cis, recruiting repressive chromatin-modifying complexes to initiate heterochromatin silencing.

- **TSIX Function:** Operating as an antisense {{< acr lncRNA >}} partner, TSIX is transcribed from the opposite strand [@Lee1999] and overlaps the XIST locus. It acts as a negative regulator of XIST. Prior to inactivation, TSIX expression on the future active X chromosome ($X_a$) represses XIST accumulation, preserving transcription.

The binary expression profiles captured in the FPKM boxplots (@fig-boxplots) — where both {{< acr lncRNA >}}s show near-zero baseline expression across all male samples — reflect this strict functional biology. Because males possess only a single, active X chromosome, the XIST/TSIX inactivation locus is never activated.

### Dosage Escape by KDM6A

The significant female bias observed in KDM6A (MSTRG.233) highlights a distinct biological phenomenon: {{< acr XCI >}} escape. KDM6A encodes a histone demethylase responsible for removing repressive H3K27me3 marks, thereby promoting transcriptionally active chromatin states.

Unlike XIST and TSIX, KDM6A maintains active transcription in male individuals. However, its elevated expression in females confirms that it escapes complete epigenetic silencing [@Balaton2015] on the inactive X chromosome. Because KDM6A is transcribed from both the active and inactive X chromosomes in females, it avoids single-dosage constraint, resulting in a higher steady-state {{< acr mRNA >}} abundance relative to males. This dual-dosage profile may contribute to sex-specific differences in immune responses and oncogenic susceptibility, as KDM6A plays a key role in chromatin remodeling.

### Conclusion

By controlling for confounding population structures via Ballgown's nested F-test framework, this study isolated true sex-linked transcriptional signals from geographic background noise. The identification of XIST, TSIX, and KDM6A validates the {{< acr RNAseq >}} processing pipeline, as these targets represent the canonical core of human X-chromosome regulation. The clear separation of population cohorts in the exploratory {{< acr PCA >}} highlights the necessity of accounting for genetic ancestry in multi-population expression studies to prevent false-positive discoveries.
